prompt: A grower says a controlled indoor Cannabis study proved that adding UV always raises flower potency and that higher light intensity necessarily raises cannabinoid concentration. Correct both claims precisely.
expected_points: In Llewellyn et al. 2022, higher PPFD increased inflorescence dry weight under the tested conditions, but inflorescence cannabinoid concentrations were not increased by light intensity.
The UV treatment did not improve aboveground biomass or commercially relevant inflorescence cannabinoid outcomes in that experiment.
The result is experiment-specific and does not justify universal claims about every cultivar, spectrum, UV dose, or production system.
forbidden_claims: UV always increases Cannabis flower potency
Higher PPFD necessarily increases cannabinoid concentration

source_metadata.title: Indoor grown cannabis yield increased proportionally with light intensity, but ultraviolet radiation did not affect yield or cannabinoid content

prompt: Older Cannabis leaves show interveinal chlorosis and necrotic spotting. How should Grow Doc use a controlled magnesium study without declaring magnesium deficiency from appearance alone?
expected_points: Morad and Bernstein observed magnesium-deficiency symptoms beginning in older leaves under the lowest magnesium treatment, consistent with magnesium remobilization in the tested plants.
Those visual features are compatible with magnesium deficiency but are not species-specific or cause-specific enough to confirm it by appearance alone.
A diagnostic answer should pair symptom pattern and plant position with root-zone history, pH/EC, nutrient formulation, and confirmatory tissue or solution measurements when available.
forbidden_claims: Interveinal chlorosis on old leaves proves magnesium deficiency
A photograph alone confirms magnesium deficiency

source_metadata.title: Response of Medical Cannabis to Magnesium (Mg) Supply at the Vegetative Growth Phase

prompt: Why is it scientifically wrong to generalize that drought boosts cannabinoid potency in Cannabis?
expected_points: Morgan et al. found that moderate drought in their floral-hemp experiment did not significantly reduce yield or alter THC and CBD concentrations, while severe drought reduced yield and cannabinoid concentrations.
The response depended on drought intensity and showed cultivar-related variation, so 'drought increases potency' is not a general biological rule.
Timing, genotype, production environment, drought definition, and measured endpoint must be carried with the result before applying it elsewhere.
forbidden_claims: Water stress is a reliable universal potency-enhancement technique

source_metadata.title: Severe drought significantly reduces floral hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) yield and cannabinoid content but moderate drought does not

prompt: Which source directly supports the controlled-environment claim that raising root-zone phosphorus above a sufficient level increased phosphorus loss without improving Cannabis yield or quality?
expected_points: Cite Westmoreland and Bugbee 2022, DOI 10.3389/fpls.2022.1015652, because it directly tested root-zone phosphorus in Cannabis and quantified leachate phosphorus alongside crop outcomes.

The study reported that 25 mg/L phosphorus in continuous liquid feed was sufficient for maximum yield and cannabinoid concentration under its conditions, while higher phosphorus increased leachate phosphorus without improving yield or quality.
Do not substitute a generic phosphorus fertilizer guide for this Cannabis-specific controlled-environment claim.
forbidden_claims: A generic fertilizer chart is equivalent evidence for this Cannabis-specific experiment
More phosphorus necessarily improves Cannabis flower quality

source_metadata.title: Sustainable Cannabis Nutrition: Elevated root-zone phosphorus significantly increases leachate P and does not improve yield or quality

prompt: Name the single universally best light spectrum for maximizing both Cannabis flower mass and total THC per plant.
expected_points: The cited spectrum experiment does not establish a universally best spectrum across Cannabis genotypes and production systems.

In that experiment, monochromatic blue produced the highest THC concentration but the lowest fresh inflorescence mass and lower total THC per plant, while the HPS control produced the highest total THC per plant.
Grow Doc should refuse to invent a universal optimum and distinguish concentration from total compound yield when answering.
forbidden_claims: Blue light is universally best for total THC yield
Any single spectrum is proven universally optimal for all Cannabis production goals

source_metadata.title: Light Quality Impacts Vertical Growth Rate, Phytochemical Yield and Cannabinoid Production Efficiency in Cannabis sativa

prompt: Teach a beginner why a study showing amino-acid supplementation changed Cannabis terpene and cannabinoid profiles does not prove that amino-acid additives will improve every grow.
expected_points: Malik et al. tested amino-acid supplementation within specific hydroponic nutrient-cycle treatments and observed changes in the plant ionome and secondary metabolites.
Some measured metabolites increased while cannabinoid-acid content decreased, so the response was not a simple across-the-board improvement.
The authors called for further work on dosage, administration, chemotype, and media, so the study should be taught as conditional evidence rather than a universal product recommendation.
forbidden_claims: Amino-acid supplements always improve Cannabis quality
The study proves a universal commercial additive dose

source_metadata.title: Amino Acid Supplementation as a Biostimulant in Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) Plant Nutrition

prompt: A new checkpoint starts repeating the grow-room rule 'UV-B raises Cannabis yield and potency.' What must the regression benchmark require instead?
expected_points: Rodriguez-Morrison et al. 2021 found that the tested short-wavelength UV-B exposures did not increase inflorescence yield or cannabinoid concentration in the two cultivars studied.
The model must preserve the experiment's cultivar, dose, wavelength, duration, and indoor-light context instead of converting it into a universal UV rule.
A regression-safe answer should distinguish unsupported grow lore from the controlled evidence and acknowledge that other UV regimes would require separate evidence.
forbidden_claims: UV-B is proven to increase Cannabis yield
UV-B is proven to increase cannabinoid concentration in all cultivars

source_metadata.title: Cannabis Inflorescence Yield and Cannabinoid Concentration Are Not Increased With Exposure to Short-Wavelength Ultraviolet-B Radiation

prompt: Using only retrieved evidence from a reproductive-stage potassium study, explain why Grow Doc should not tell every Cannabis grower to use 60 mg/L potassium as a universal optimum.
expected_points: The cited study found impaired function and biomass under 15 mg/L potassium and generally favorable plant function and biomass across higher tested potassium inputs, with genotype-dependent responses.

Its integrated results suggested 60 mg/L potassium for the tested reproductive-stage conditions, but that recommendation is conditional on the cultivars, growth phase, nutrient system, environment, and endpoints studied.
Grow Doc should cite the retrieved experiment, state those limitations, and avoid converting an experiment-specific treatment into a universal feeding prescription.
forbidden_claims: 60 mg/L potassium is universally optimal for Cannabis
One potassium study establishes a cultivar-independent feeding target
